_meta.title: CNC machining starting parameters by material
_meta.disclaimer: Starting points only. Adjust for machine rigidity, tool geometry, holder, and workholding. Verify before cutting production parts.

units.feed_rate_note: mm/min = RPM x flutes x feed_per_tooth

aluminum.tooling: 2-3 flute carbide, uncoated or ZrN; polished flutes for chip evacuation
aluminum.coolant: Flood, mist, or air blast; air is fine for finishing
aluminum.notes: The default alloy. Machines clean at high RPM. Deep pockets need strong chip evacuation or you will recut chips and wreck the finish.

aluminum.tooling: Sharp carbide, 2-3 flute; keep tools fresh
aluminum.notes: Around 30% higher yield than 6061 and noticeably more abrasive on tooling. Tool wear runs 20-30% faster than 6061. Anodizes darker and less uniformly.
Gummy compared with 6061. Keep the feed up so the tool cuts instead of rubbing, and use a lubricating coolant rather than plain water.

stainless_steel.tooling: AlTiN or TiAlN coated carbide, 4-5 flute for rigidity
stainless_steel.notes: Work-hardens fast. Never dwell or rub — if the tool stops moving it hardens the surface and kills the next pass. Rigid setup matters more than speed here.
Harder to machine than 304 and more prone to work-hardening and galling. Common in medical and marine parts — expect longer cycle times and budget for them.
Machine in Condition A (solution treated) then age harden to H900/H1025. Machining after hardening is possible but expensive — plan the sequence.

titanium.tooling: Sharp uncoated or AlTiN carbide; positive rake; never a worn tool
titanium.coolant: High-pressure flood — heat must leave with the chip
titanium.notes: Low thermal conductivity means heat stays in the cut and in the tool. Conservative speeds, sharp edges, and generous coolant. Thin walls deflect — light radial engagements. Not a material to learn on.
Softer and gummier than Grade 5. Prone to galling and built-up edge — keep the feed up and the tool sharp.

copper_brass.tooling: Sharp carbide, high rake; polished flutes
copper_brass.notes: Sticky and abrasive. Chip control is the whole game — peck and clear. Thermal conductivity pulls heat into the part, so watch dimensions on thin features.

copper_brass.coolant: Mist or flood; often run dry with air blast
copper_brass.notes: One of the easiest materials to machine. Free-cutting. Small chips — manage them so they do not pack into fixtures.

steel.tooling: TiAlN or AlTiN coated carbide, 4 flute
steel.notes: 1045 is harder and less forgiving than 1018. Both machine predictably with coated carbide. Watch for stringy chips in low carbon grades.
Machines well annealed (28-32 HRC). Above 35 HRC, move to harder tooling and reduce speeds — or plan for a hard-milling setup.

engineering_plastics.tooling: Sharp polished carbide, 2-3 flute; high rake
engineering_plastics.coolant: Air blast or mist — flood optional
engineering_plastics.notes: Machines like a hard plastic but moves after cutting. Stress relieve or anneal before finishing critical dimensions. Sharp tools and generous clearance prevent melting and burrs.

engineering_plastics.tooling: Diamond-coated or PCD carbide — abrasive filler destroys standard coatings
engineering_plastics.notes: Filler is highly abrasive: expect much shorter tool life. Use PCD or diamond coating for any real volume.

engineering_plastics.tooling: Very sharp carbide, high rake, polished flutes
engineering_plastics.notes: Soft and slippery — it deflects away from the tool rather than cutting. Sharp tools, light passes, rigid support. Prone to burrs and dimensional movement.
Machines clean. Glass-filled grades behave like filled PEEK — abrasive, shorter tool life.
Hard and brittle. Chips break fine — contain them. Coolant contact can cause stress cracking in some grades, so many shops cut it dry with air blast.
Similar to PEEK in behavior but less expensive. Watch for stress crazing if coolant chemistry is wrong.
Free-machining and dimensionally stable. Do not let it get hot — it can outgas formaldehyde when overheated. Great material for fixtures and test parts.
Tougher and stiffer than PTFE, so it machines better. Common in semiconductor wet benches and chemical handling.
